etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English hatrede, hatreden (“hatred”), from hate (“hate”) + -rede (“suffix denoting state or condition”), equivalent to hate +‎ -red; compare sibred, Scots luferent. Related to Icelandic hatri (“hatred”).

quote.citation: 1697, [William] Congreve, The Mourning Bride, a Tragedy. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, Act III, page 39:
quote.text: Heav'n has no Rage, like Love to Hatred turn'd, / Nor Hell a Fury, like a Woman ſcorn'd.

quote.citation: 1748, David Hume, Enquiries concerning the human understanding and concerning the principles of moral., London: Oxford University Press, published 1973, § 34:
quote.text: the very circumstance which renders it so innocent is what chiefly exposes it to the public hatred

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, chapter 8, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC:
quote.text: It was a casual sneer, obviously one of a long line. There was hatred behind it, but of a quiet, chronic type, nothing new or unduly virulent, and he was taken aback by the flicker of amazed incredulity that passed over the younger man's ravaged face.
Fears and hatreds pay no attention to facts.
